extracted.intended_audience: mathematics-education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and criteria for analyzing undergraduate students' mathematical reasoning, including proof-writing (using Toulmin's model), understanding of limits (Cottrill's genetic decomposition plus additional strands), and the negotiation/legitimization of sociomathematical norms in classroom discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin argumentation elements (data, warrant, backing, qualifier, conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze mathematical arguments (including instructor-written proofs and student work) by categorizing each argument element as data, warrant, backing, qualifier, or conclusion per Toulmin (1969).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Toulmin's model to code written and spoken components of proofs; note that spoken warrants/backing may not appear in written student work. The paper used counts of each element in instructor and student work to compare modeling and appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident logging criteria for proof-production/presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Log an incident as proof-production/presentation when any class member is writing or showing a formal mathematical proof that draws on symbolic notation and logical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to classroom video: record episodes that include proof-writing or presentation; include whether aspects of argumentation were written or spoken aloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor modeling expectations for proof-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize what the instructor models when writing proofs (which elements are written vs spoken): e.g., Dr. Tripp always wrote data and conclusion, rarely wrote warrants, and never wrote backing or qualifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret instructor's mixed written/spoken modeling as setting implicit expectations for students: strong expectation to write data and conclusion, inconsistent modeling for warrants, and low expectation for backing or qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of instructor's modeled proof-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether students have appropriated the proof-writing behaviors modeled by the instructor by checking whether student proofs include the same argumentation elements (data, warrants, backing, qualifiers, conclusions) at similar rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare aggregate counts (written vs implied) from student work to instructor modeling. Example: students almost universally wrote data and conclusion, included written warrants less often, and almost never wrote backing or qualifiers—matching instructor's written model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Toulmin analysis to link instruction and student learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Toulmin’s framework not only to analyze student work but also to analyze classroom instruction and classroom dialogue to explain relationships between what instructors model and what students do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toulmin analysis can reveal mismatches (e.g., instructors speaking warrants but not writing them) and predict corresponding student behaviors; useful for designing meta-level classroom dialogue to make expectations explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cottrill 7-Step Genetic Decomposition (stages of limit understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify student understanding of limits according to the 7-step genetic decomposition (Cottrill et al., 1996), which emphasizes progression from an x-value understanding toward the formal definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary coding framework in interview analysis; the paper found interviewees reached no higher than step 3. The authors note limitations of this decomposition in accounting for methods, examples, and justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method sophistication strand for limit understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the sophistication of the method a student selects for evaluating a limit (e.g., graphs, tables, algebraic manipulation, recognizing continuity, application of L'Hôpital's rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of a more sophisticated or conceptually powerful method (e.g., recognizing derivative implies continuity) is evidence of stronger understanding; different valid methods exist and choice reflects understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification quality strand for limit understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the student's ability to correctly use and justify the chosen method based on perceived applicable information (accuracy of computations and logical justification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct method with incorrect computation counts as failure of justification. Graphical examples/counterexamples and high-level justifications are assessed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability strand for limit understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the student's ability to see the relevance and applicability of given data and their own knowledge in the context of the problem (i.e., recognizing which examples/counterexamples or facts apply to the task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes students who construct appropriate counterexamples and apply them to disprove statements from those who fail to see applicability; critical for diagnosing understanding beyond procedural skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-strand model for student comprehension of the limit concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed model that supplements the genetic decomposition with at least three strands: method for solving the task, justification for the solution, and applicability of method and justification within the problem context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend incorporating these strands into assessments to better diagnose student understanding and guide instruction; further research needed to validate and refine strands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four components of a sociomathematical norm
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a sociomathematical norm, four components must be identified: (1) a mathematical expectation is set forth, (2) a mathematical interpretation of the expectation occurs, (3) the expectation is agreed upon, and (4) the expectation is validated as legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms are negotiated and re-negotiated by classroom participants; researcher/teacher/student-perceived norms may differ (teacher-endorsed vs enacted vs student-perceived). Use the four components to detect whether an expectation has become a sociomathematical norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority relation components (bearer, receiver, legitimacy, change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize authority in the classroom by an authority relation: at least one bearer of authority makes a claim; the receiver recognizes the claim as legitimate and is influenced to change behavior (legitimacy and change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish traditional hierarchical authority (teacher as bearer) from more fluid authority relations in inquiry-based settings; legitimacy is key to whether norms influence behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority legitimizing classroom norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of authority that legitimize classroom claims/norms: Hierarchal (position-based), Expertise (perceived or demonstrated expertise/ownership), Mathematical (legitimized by argument and justification), and Performative (ability to engage the class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These authorities can be held by either instructors or students; analyze which type(s) are invoked when new expectations or norms are introduced and negotiated.
